newsitem.title: FRANCE: French privatisations heading for a rough patch.
newsitem.headline: French privatisations heading for a rough patch.

text.p: Whatever the outcome of the parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, France's privatisation programme is heading for a rough patch.

While the Socialist opposition has told voters it will not continue with privatisations, it may be forced to sell off assets to pay for urgently needed injections of capital into other state-owned firms, economists say.

Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin this week softened his stance on the largest of these sales -- that of a stake in telecommunations monopoly France Telecom, saying he would first consult the company's staff. The party had previously said it opposed the sale.

A centre-right government wants to continue the privatisation programme, with Prime Minister Alain Juppe saying in a newspaper interview published on Thursday that bank Credit Lyonnais and airline Air France could be sold this year.
But the easier-to-sell companies will have gone after the scheduled sale of a minority stake in France Telecom in June and a 58 percent stake in defence electronics group Thomson-CSF in the summer.
Further state sales also risk hitting increasing opposition from labour unions and large sections of the public that appear to vigorously defend the role of the state in France's mixed economy.

A speeded up privatisation programme is unlikely to have an effect on France's bid to meet the European single currency targets that require a cut in the budget deficit to no more than three percent of GDP this year because sale revenues cannot be used to cut the deficit.
The revenues do help to cut the national debt but France is already well placed to meet the debt criterion in the single currency's guiding Masstricht treaty of no more debt than 60 percent of GDP.
Privatisation revenues can, however, be used to cover expenses such as a capital boost to other state companies which could otherwise drain the budget and weigh on debt.
France will need some 20 billion francs ($3.5 billion) for insurance group GAN and at least 11 billion francs for consumer electronics group Thomson Multimedia (TMM).
Credit Lyonnais, which has already received massive aid, could need another eight to 12 billion francs.
Economists have speculated that a new privatisation, or partial sale, might present an opportunity for a special deal such as the France Telecom pension transfer.
There the state received 37.5 billion francs from France Telecom in exchange for taking over the pension liabilities of the staff retaining civil servant status.
But they say it is unclear whether any status change at the EDF/GDF utility group, SNCF state railways, or the Poste postal services could give rise to a similar operation.
Centre-right governments have raised 155 billion francs in privatisations and partial sales since the 1993 Rhone-Poulenc SA sale under Prime Minister Edouard Balladur.

What is left is insurer CNP, with an estimated value of 10 billion francs, financially recovering aeroengine maker Snecma and a stake in nuclear engineering group Framatome which involves far more than just money.
Bank Banque Hervet could raise some 800 to 900 million francs while the sale of Societe Marseillaise de Credit could fall far short of the three billion francs it has cost in capital injections.

The sale of the SFP film studios are set to be concluded at a loss and further sales of shares in computer group Cie des Machines Bull would still not add up to the 11 billion francs in capital injections it has received since 1993.

The big ticket item is France Telecom. The government aims to raise 30 to 50 billion francs through the sale of 30-35 percent, with financial analysts having valued the group at between 160 and 210 billion francs in April.
A 58-percent stake in Thomson-CSF, to be sold either to Alcatel Alsthom and Dassault or to Lagardere Groupe, could net more than 30 billion francs.
The value of Credit Lyonnais is difficult to estimate due to the pending recapitalisation, its profit recovery and the possible effect of further forced asset sales.

But based on a crude price/earnings ratio of 12 for Societe Generale and Banque Nationale de Paris and expected average 1997 and 1998 profits of some 1.5 billion francs, Credit Lyonnais would be worth 18 billion francs.
A report on Thursday alleging massive fraud within Credit Lyonnais before a previous government rescue package in 1993 involved former subsidiaries and is not relevant.

Air France aims to break even this year and have a profit of 500 million francs in 1997/98. According to Reuters Securities 3000, Germany's Lufthansa is trading at 17.21 times its expected 1997 profit, which would give Air France an estimated market value of 8.6 billion francs.
But a complicating factor is an Air France strike that was on its third day on Thursday and is reported to be possibly costing the company up to 100 million francs a day. ($ = 5.712 French Francs)
